Neighborhood Builders Fast Track - Homepage














          Share

About Neighborhood Builders

Announced as part of Mayor Mamdani’s first 100 days, the Neighborhood Builders Fast Track is a new, expedited process to speed the delivery of affordable housing on City-owned land. Through Neighborhood Builders, HPD will pre-qualify M/WBE and non-profit affordable housing builders and shorten the Request for Proposals (RFP) process for certain projects by several months. These time savings will be achieved be establishing a pre-qualified list of M/WBE and non-profit developers through the Neighborhood Builders Request for Qualifications (RFQ) released on March 25, 2026. Pre-qualified developers will be invited off the list to patriciate in an expedited RFP process.

Non-profit organizations and certified M/WBE firms who wish to be considered for sites via the Neighborhood Builders RFQ can learn more about the process on the Neighborhood Builders Fast Track RFQ Webpage.




Fast Track RFP Process






1. Community Visioning 


The Community Visioning phase is your chance to help shape the Request for Proposals (RFP) for the new affordable housing and community amenities at each site. HPD will conduct engagement events and surveys for each individual Neighborhood Builders site. Takeaways for each site will be published in a document attached to the RFP.  

2. Open Request 


HPD will issue an RFP that seeks development proposals for each Neighborhood Builders site. Development teams will propose projects in response to the criteria and requirements outlined in the document.  

3. Submissions Review 


HPD will evaluate development proposals based on their ability to meet the requirements and advance the goals described in the RFP document and the CVR.  

4. Developer Designation 

The development team with the strongest proposal will be selected by HPD to proceed with the development.  

5. Public Approvals 


The project will go through the City's public approval process and secure financing before construction can begin. Some projects may already have prior land use approvals in place, or may utilize expedited processes such as those described on HPD’s Expediting New Affordable Housing webpage.  

6. Construction 

The proposed affordable housing building will be constructed.  

7. Housing Lottery 


When construction is almost complete, the new affordable homes will be made available through HPD's lottery process on NYC Housing Connect.  

How to Get Involved

 Follow the links for each site below to learn more about how to get involved.




Fall 2026 Sites

HPD launched the Community Visioning phase for the following three sites in Fall 2026. All three sites were identified in the Land Inventory Fast Track (LIFT) Tracker released in July, 2026. Follow the links for each site below to learn more about how to get involved. 


Expand AllCollapse All



784-800 Myrtle Ave, Brooklyn



784-800 Myrtle Ave, Brooklyn

Identified in the 2020 Bedford-Stuyvesant Housing plan, 784-800 Myrtle Ave is a vacant City-owned site in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn.



109-43 Farmers Blvd, Queens



109-43 Farmers Blvd, Queens

HPD committed to building affordable homeownership opportunities on this site as part of the 2025 Jamaica Neighborhood Plan. The site is located in St. Albans, Queens, and includes three vacant one-story buildings.



1337 Jerome Ave, The Bronx



1337 Jerome Ave, The Bronx

HPD committed to building affordable homeownership opportunities on this site as part of the 2024 City of Yes for Housing Opportunity zoning text amendment. The site is located in the Mount Eden neighborhood of the Bronx, and includes a vacant one-story commercial building.


Frequently Asked Questions  


Neighborhood Builders Fast Track Request for Proposals (RFPs)






Expand AllCollapse All


Click a topic, or press the enter key on a topic, to reveal its answer.


What is a Request for Proposals (RFP)?



A Request for Proposals is a document issued by HPD that seeks proposals for new housing and community amenities on City-owned land. Development teams submit proposals and those proposals are evaluated based on their ability to meet the requirements and advance the goals identified in the RFP and community engagement report.



What is the difference between the Neighborhood Builders Fast Track RFQ and RFPs?



A Request for Qualifications (RFQ) is a solicitation process designed to pre-qualify developers who meet criteria related to experience and capacity. HPD uses the Neighborhood Builders RFQ to build a list of vetted non-profit and M/WBE partners qualified to work on affordable housing development, including for certain RFP sites.



Why is HPD issuing RFPs on these sites?



Many New Yorkers are experiencing homelessness, living in poor quality housing, or struggling to keep up with housing costs. A priority for the mayoral administration is for HPD to finance and preserve more affordable housing, and to enable new affordable housing developments to include important community amenities. The Neighborhood Builders Fast Track initiative provides an opportunity for the City to create 100% affordable housing that will serve the community and New Yorkers in a more expediated manner.



How is the Neighborhood Builders RFP different than a typical RFP released by HPD, and how will it result in a faster process?



A typical HPD Request for Proposals (RFP) is a competitive process in which HPD calls for developers to submit site-specific project proposals that respond to a set of defined goals and guidelines that are informed by policy goals and feedback from the community. Under the Neighborhood Builders Initiative, a Request for Qualifications (RFQ) identifies a set of criteria for developers to be evaluated to establish a list of qualified developers to potentially be selected to develop, or to apply to develop, a site for affordable housing development.

The pre-qualification process, as well as working with simpler sites that may have prior commitments or land use approvals, will reduce the time taken to designate sites to developers for certain projects by approximately seven to eight months. The Neighborhood Builders Fast Track Initiative, in addition to other streamlined processes such as the Expedited Land Use Review Procedure (ELURP), would reduce the overall pre-development process by approximately 2.5 years.



Can the community help choose the developers or proposal for an RFP site?



We highly value community input informing the development of the RFP before it is written and issued, which is why we designed a questionnaire and will be hosting a workshop to gather your input. HPD takes the integrity of its RFP competitive review process seriously. As such, HPD is required to ensure that the RFP process prevents potential conflicts of interest (and disqualifications of teams because of potential conflict of interest) and cannot allow community members to partake in the review.

As stated above, the input gathered throughout the engagement process is published in the report and attached to the RFP for development teams to refer to in crafting proposals. Proposals will be scored in part on how well they respond to the visions of the community.



Will we be able to see the RFPs when they are released?



Yes. The RFP and any relevant supplemental information will be linked on the sites individual project website to downloadable as PDFs. 


Community Input


How will community input be incorporated into the RFP?



The results of the community engagement will be summarized in a report. The report is provided as part of the RFP document so that prospective developers can understand and craft proposals that are responsive to the priorities and needs of the community. Amongst other evaluation criteria, proposals will be evaluated in part on how thoughtfully they consider and respond to the priorities and needs. (See what sites are open in your neighborhood.)



Why is the community engagement phase shortened compared to HPD’s typical RFP



Sites under the Neighborhood Builders initiative are considered ready-to-develop, meaning they are small-to-moderately sized with more programmatic constraints and may have outstanding prior commitments from neighborhood plans and citywide initiatives. HPD is committed to delivering on these commitments in an expedited manner. HPD will work closely with local community stakeholders to help spread the word about upcoming projects.



Will community members who are not able to attend in-person meetings have an opportunity to provide input?



Yes. For people who are not able to make it to public events, there is an online Project Questionnaire available on a project site’s website. Community members can also offer feedback and submit questions about this project by emailing the project site email address. For community members without access to the internet, there will be paper versions of the project questionnaire available at our public tabling events.

HPD will present our findings at a public report back meeting when the community visioning phase is coming to an end.



Will there be additional opportunities for community feedback after a developer is selected for a site?



Yes. The community engagement process does not end with the release of the report. Once selected, the developer and HPD will report back to the Community Board and other key stakeholders about project progress toward major milestones and how to apply for affordable housing.



Will input from people who live far away from the site have the same weight as people near the site?



While we receive input from many different types of stakeholders, our goal is to focus on the big picture and to accommodate as many perspectives as possible. We are conducting extensive outreach in the community to ensure that those who may be most impacted by the new development are informed and have opportunities to provide feedback.



Once the building is complete, how can I apply to live in one of the units?



After construction, newly available apartments go through a housing lottery process. Visit NYC Housing Connect online for more information about current affordable housing lotteries. Supportive housing and formerly homeless units are leased through referrals from the New York City Department of Homeless Services (DHS), Human Resources Administration (HRA), HPD, or other sources.

For help on how to apply for housing, contact a nearby NYC Housing Ambassador Brooklyn.
